\chapter{Answering With More Than Yes}
\label{ch:te-replies}
\hlchaptermodality{49}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can answer in Telugu with more than yes and no --- true, enough, certainly, perhaps, just so --- and see the three-vowel grid running under \te{అది}, \te{ఇక్కడ} and \te{ఎలా}.}

Complete TE-C49-alright and demonstrate the chapter promise.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[nijaṁ]{\te{నిజం} (nijaṁ) — true; the truth}

\label{lesson:TE-C49-true}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run: what did \emph{atithi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{నిజం}}
\textbf{\te{నిజం}} (\emph{nijaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}true; the truth\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{nija} meant \textquotedblleft{}one's own, innate\textquotedblright{} — what belongs to a thing by its nature. Telugu moved it one step: what belongs to a thing by nature is what is really so, and \te{నిజం} became the truth.

Alone it answers a doubt: \emph{nijaṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}true\textquotedblright{}. With a question on the end it becomes perhaps the commonest interjection in the language: \emph{nijamā?}, \textquotedblleft{}really?\textquotedblright{}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five answers that are neither \te{అవును} nor \te{లేదు}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nijaṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{nijaṁ}, then \emph{nijamā?}, and say which one asks
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{నిజం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}true; the truth\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cālu]{\te{చాలు} (cālu) — enough, that will do}

\label{lesson:TE-C49-enough}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{nijaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{చాలు}}
\textbf{\te{చాలు}} (\emph{cālu}) — \textquotedblleft{}enough, that will do\textquotedblright{}.

\te{చాలు} is a verb — \textquotedblleft{}it suffices\textquotedblright{} — used as a complete answer. Held over a glass being filled it stops the pouring; said of an argument it ends it.

\te{చాలా}, the everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}very\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}a lot\textquotedblright{}, is the same root wearing a different ending. Sufficiency and abundance sit one letter apart, which is a fair account of how the two ideas are related anywhere.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cālu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{cālu}, then \emph{nijaṁ}, and say which one you would use to stop someone pouring
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{చాలు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}enough, that will do\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tappakuṇḍā]{\te{తప్పకుండా} (tappakuṇḍā) — certainly, without fail}

\label{lesson:TE-C49-certainly}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{cālu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{తప్పకుండా}}
\textbf{\te{తప్పకుండా}} (\emph{tappakuṇḍā}) — \textquotedblleft{}certainly, without fail\textquotedblright{}.

Take it apart: \te{తప్పు}, \textquotedblleft{}to miss, to slip, to go wrong\textquotedblright{}, plus \textbf{-\te{కుండా}}, the ending meaning \textquotedblleft{}without doing\textquotedblright{}. \te{తప్పకుండా} is \emph{without missing}.

The ending is worth having on its own, because it attaches to any verb stem: \emph{ceppakuṇḍā}, without telling; \emph{tinakuṇḍā}, without eating. One suffix, and every verb you own gains a negative.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tappakuṇḍā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{tappakuṇḍā}, then \emph{cālu}, and say which one is a promise
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{తప్పకుండా} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}certainly, without fail\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ēmō]{\te{ఏమో} (ēmō) — perhaps, who knows}

\label{lesson:TE-C49-perhaps}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{tappakuṇḍā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{ఏమో}}
\textbf{\te{ఏమో}} (\emph{ēmō}) — \textquotedblleft{}perhaps, who knows\textquotedblright{}.

\te{ఏమో} is a shrug made into a word: perhaps, it may be so, who knows.

Look at the front of it and you will find the questioning \te{ఏ}- that already stands in \te{ఏమిటి}, \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}. \te{ఏమో} is that question with the asking taken out and only the uncertainty left behind.

It also hangs on the end of a whole sentence, where English would need a separate clause: \emph{vastāḍēmō}, \textquotedblleft{}he may come\textquotedblright{}. A language with a settled, unembarrassed word for not knowing is telling you something about its manners.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ēmō}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ēmō}, then \emph{tappakuṇḍā}, and say which one commits you
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{ఏమో} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}perhaps, who knows\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[alāgē]{\te{అలాగే} (alāgē) — just so, alright then}

\label{lesson:TE-C49-alright}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ēmō} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{అలాగే}}
\textbf{\te{అలాగే}} (\emph{alāgē}) — \textquotedblleft{}just so, alright then\textquotedblright{}.

\te{అలా} means \textquotedblleft{}in that way\textquotedblright{}; \textbf{-\te{గే}} is the small emphatic tail that makes it \textquotedblleft{}just so\textquotedblright{}. \te{అలాగే} is the yes you give to an instruction — not \textquotedblleft{}that is correct\textquotedblright{} but \textquotedblleft{}it shall be as you said\textquotedblright{}.

Now look at the front of it. \te{అ}- points far, and already carries \te{అది}, \textquotedblleft{}that one\textquotedblright{}, and \te{అక్కడ}, \textquotedblleft{}there\textquotedblright{}. \te{ఇ}- points near: \te{ఇది}, \te{ఇక్కడ}, and so \te{ఇలా}, \textquotedblleft{}in this way\textquotedblright{}. \te{ఎ}- asks: \te{ఎక్కడ}, \te{ఎలా}. Three vowels, one grid, and \te{అలాగే} is simply the far corner of it with an ending stuck on.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five answers, and a three-way grid you can now see running under \te{అది}, \te{ఇక్కడ} and \te{ఎలా}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{alāgē}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then say \emph{alāgē} as a reply to \emph{dayacēsi kūrcō}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{అలాగే} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}just so, alright then\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
